stem: A union-represented nurse wants to challenge a disciplinary action that is covered by the nurse's collective-bargaining agreement. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Discuss the issue only informally with coworkers because negotiated grievance procedures should not be used for covered disciplinary disputes.
options.B: Assume the same grievance steps and deadlines apply in every workplace, regardless of the collective-bargaining agreement.
options.C: Review and use the grievance procedure provided by the applicable collective-bargaining agreement, following any specified steps and time limits and seeking union representation or assistance as appropriate.
options.D: Resign immediately because disciplinary actions covered by a collective-bargaining agreement cannot be reviewed through a grievance process.

rationale: The National Labor Relations Act recognizes employee grievances and treats final adjustment by a method agreed on by the parties as the desirable method for resolving disputes arising from the application or interpretation of an existing collective-bargaining agreement. The NLRB also recognizes a union's duty of fair representation when handling grievances. Because procedures differ by agreement, the nurse should use the applicable negotiated process and follow its actual requirements rather than assume a universal procedure. C is therefore the best answer.
educational_objective: Recognize that a union-represented employee challenging a matter covered by a collective-bargaining agreement should use the agreement-specific grievance process rather than assume universal rules or bypass the negotiated procedure.
source_document_title: National Labor Relations Act; Right to fair representation
source_version_date: Current federal statutory text and NLRB guidance; accessed 2026-08-16
source_locator: NLRA Section 9(a) — employee grievances and bargaining representative; Section 203(d) — final adjustment by a method agreed upon by the parties for grievance disputes arising under an existing collective-bargaining agreement; NLRB Right to fair representation — handling grievances
source_claim_supported: Federal labor law recognizes grievances and negotiated dispute-resolution methods under collective-bargaining agreements; unions have a duty of fair representation when handling grievances, while specific procedures depend on the applicable agreement.

source_original.stem: A union-represented nurse wants to challenge a disciplinary action covered by the collective-bargaining agreement. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Discuss the issue only with coworkers because negotiated grievance procedures should not be used
options.B: Assume every workplace uses identical grievance rules regardless of the applicable labor agreement
options.C: Use the negotiated grievance or appeal process and follow the agreement's documented steps and timelines
options.D: Resign immediately because a covered disciplinary decision cannot be reviewed through a grievance process

source_original.rationale: When a collective-bargaining agreement provides a grievance procedure for a disciplinary dispute, the employee should use the negotiated process and its required steps, representation rights, and timelines. Procedures vary by agreement and law.
source_original.source_detail: NLRA Sections 9(a) and 203(d): employee grievances and agreed grievance-dispute resolution under collective-bargaining agreements; accessed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Kept the collective-bargaining grievance construct but removed unsupported universal representation/timeline language: the final answer now says to follow any steps/time limits specified by the actual agreement and seek representation as appropriate. Added NLRB fair-representation guidance and reduced difficulty from hard to medium.

audit_findings.source_authority: NLRB official federal statutory text and employee-rights guidance; NCSBN 2026 Test Plan
audit_findings.claim_audit: Sections 9(a) and 203(d) support grievances and agreed dispute-resolution methods; fair-representation guidance supports union grievance handling. Agreement-specific details are not universalized.

distractor_audit.A: Contradicts the recognized role of negotiated grievance procedures.
distractor_audit.C: Correct and carefully limited to the applicable agreement.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect; covered disputes may be addressed through grievance processes.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only C uses the agreement-specific mechanism recognized by federal labor law.
audit_findings.cueing: All alternatives are responses to a covered disciplinary dispute; answer depends on legal-management knowledge.
audit_findings.blueprint: Management of Care retained under legal rights/responsibilities and management concepts. NCLEX relevance is narrower than core bedside content but remains a defensible management/legal workplace construct because the stem explicitly limits the issue to a collective-bargaining agreement.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Re-read NLRA 9(a), 203(d), and NLRB fair-representation guidance, challenged whether timelines/representation could be universalized, narrowed those claims, and confirmed C remained uniquely correct.
